summary:
Helios is a decision-support platform for planning and monitoring humanitarian shelter sites, grounded in real NASA Earth-observation data instead of simulation.
Displaced people often arrive at sites chosen under emergency pressure, without full risk assessment, and conditions go unmonitored afterward. 
We use NASA/ISRO's NISAR L-band SAR satellite, which sees through clouds and darkness, to flag real surface change between passes as a prompt for human review, never an automated verdict. Mae La's sector boundaries are anchored to a real OpenStreetMap footprint, hand-checked against actual radar imagery. Elevation and
  HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) come from a real public DEM via our own priority-flood and D8 flow-routing pipeline, feeding a fully transparent flood score (score = sum of weight times factor, auditable by anyone). That same real terrain drives where water, medical, and food points go: safest ground for critical services, lowest ground near natural drainage for water.
Every value is labeled real or simulated, and the map shows only aggregated sector population, never individual shelter locations, to protect a vulnerable population.

Helios shows free, open NASA data can make humanitarian planning safer, faster, and auditable.
details:
Helios is a web dashboard that turns real NASA Earth-observation data into actionable risk and planning information for humanitarian shelter sites.

How it works: NASA/ISRO's NISAR L-band SAR satellite images each camp every 12 days, through clouds and in darkness. Our pipeline streams only the relevant chunks of each product, compares passes within the same track/orbit, and flags sectors where backscatter changed beyond noise - a prompt for human review, never a confirmed verdict on what changed. Elevation and HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) come from a public DEM, run through our own priority-flood and D8 flow-routing pipeline, feeding a fully transparent flood score (score = sum of weight times factor, auditable line by line). A live 7-day forecast feeds the same score. That real terrain also drives facility placement: water points go near natural drainage, medical and food points go on the highest, safest ground in each sector. Mae La's sector grid is clipped to its real boundary from OpenStreetMap, hand-verified against the actual radar imagery.

Benefits: works when optical satellites can't (monsoon cloud cover, night), every number is auditable instead of a black box, and facility siting is grounded in measured terrain instead of guesswork.

Impact: faster, evidence-based decisions for organizations like UNHCR or TBC before and during flood season, and a model that scales to any camp since every data source (NISAR, DEM, OpenStreetMap, weather) is free and public.

Tools: React, TypeScript, TanStack Start, MapLibre GL JS; Python, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, earthaccess, pyproj. deployed on Netlify.

Creativity: we wrote our own hydrology pipeline instead of using packaged GIS tools, and cross-checked simulated sector placement against real radar imagery pixel by pixel, correcting it until it matched the camp's true footprint.

Factors considered: never expose individual shelter locations, only aggregated sector data; label every value real or simulated; and keep the app working even if a live data source fails.
